title: Night Guard Round
story: A hotel's corridor is a loop. The rooms along it are numbered in increasing order, and after the highest-numbered room the loop comes back to the lowest. Each night the guard starts the round at a different room and walks the whole loop once, ticking off rooms on a sheet.
So tonight's sheet might read 410, 415, 502, 517, 108, 112, 230, 301: sorted, except that it wraps around once. A guest calls about room 112. Where on the sheet is it?
task: Write findRoom(round, room). round holds distinct room numbers: a strictly increasing list that may have been rotated (some prefix moved to the back). Return the index of room in round, or -1 if it is not there.
The rotation may be zero, so the list may be fully sorted. An empty list returns -1. Aim for O(log n).
constraints: All room numbers are different; round is an increasing list rotated by some amount.

examples.explanation: The sheet climbs from 410 to 517, wraps, and climbs again from 108 to 301. Room 112 is in the second climb, at index 5.
300 would belong in the second climb between 230 and 301, but there is no room 300.

hints: Cut the first example in half at index 3: [410, 415, 502, 517] and [108, 112, 230, 301]. Is one of the halves sorted? Pick other cut points. Is one side always sorted?
Yes: wherever you cut, at least one side contains no wrap, so it is a normal sorted run. You can tell which by comparing its two ends.
On the sorted side you can check in O(1) whether room lies between its first and last value. If it does, search there. If not, it can only be on the other side.

Standard lo/hi loop. At mid: if it is the room, return. If round[lo] <= round[mid], the left part is sorted: go left when round[lo] <= room < round[mid], else go right. Otherwise the right part is sorted: go right when round[mid] < room <= round[hi], else go left.
bruteForce: Read the sheet from the top until you find the room. O(n), up to 100,000 checks.
Plain binary search does not work either: it assumes the whole list is sorted. Searching for 112 in the example, it sees 517 in the middle, decides 112 must be to the left, and never finds it.

py: def find_room(round: list[int], room: int) -> int:

tests.note: the round starts at the lowest room
only the first room is before the wrap
only the last room is after the wrap
the room right after the wrap
the room right before the wrap
two rooms: lo and mid coincide

js: // lo..mid has no wrap: it is sorted
if (round[lo] <= room && room < round[mid]) hi = mid - 1;
// mid..hi has no wrap: it is sorted
if (round[mid] < room && room <= round[hi]) lo = mid + 1;
py: # lo..mid has no wrap: it is sorted
# mid..hi has no wrap: it is sorted
walkthrough: The list wraps at most once, so any cut leaves at least one side that is plainly sorted. Find that side by comparing its ends, ask whether the room fits inside its range, and keep the half that can hold it.
• lo = 0, hi = 7, mid = 3 (517). 410 ≤ 517, so the left side 410..517 is sorted. 112 is not between 410 and 517, so it must be on the right. lo = 4.

A search for 301 takes longer: at mid = 3 the left is sorted and 301 is outside 410..517, so lo = 4; at mid = 5 (112), 108 ≤ 112 so the left 108..112 is sorted, 301 is outside, lo = 6; at mid = 6 (230) the left is sorted, 301 is outside, lo = 7; and mid = 7 finds it.

Watch the <= in round[lo] <= round[mid]. When only two rooms are left, lo and mid are the same index. With a strict <, the code would decide the right side is sorted when it is not, and the two-room tests fail.
solution.timeWhy: Each round discards half the remaining range.
solution.takeaway: Binary search only needs a way to rule out half the range each step, not a fully sorted list. In a rotated list, one half is always sorted; test whether the target fits in that half's range and discard the other.
